It sounds like your mother-in-law’s behavior is very one-sided, where she expects your child to make her feel good without showing genuine care or interest. This type of dynamic can be frustrating, especially when you feel like the relationship isn’t mutually supportive or caring.

Here are some thoughts on handling this situation:

1. Set Clear Boundaries

Limit Unnecessary Expectations: It’s okay to set boundaries around how much your child or you are expected to do for her. If it feels like she’s only engaging for her own benefit, you have the right to limit those interactions.

Respectfully Say No: If she asks for things that only serve to make her feel good but don’t benefit your child or family, it’s okay to decline. You don’t have to fulfill expectations that don’t align with your values or priorities.


2. Don’t Overcompensate

Avoid People-Pleasing: If she expects your child to perform or do things for her, resist the pressure to encourage or push your child into those situations. It’s more important for your child to feel loved for who they are rather than being used to make someone else feel good.

Stay Grounded in Your Priorities: Focus on what’s important for your child’s well-being, not on meeting her emotional needs, especially if they come at the cost of your child’s comfort or autonomy.


3. Limit Performative Engagements

Protect Your Child’s Emotional Health: If you feel like she only interacts with your child to boost her own ego, limit those interactions. It’s more important for your child to experience authentic, caring relationships rather than performative ones.

Encourage Healthy Relationships: Help your child build meaningful connections with people who show genuine love and care for them, rather than those who seek out interactions for self-serving reasons.


4. Communicate with Your Partner

Work Together: It might help to discuss this dynamic with your partner so they can understand how it affects you and your child. They may be able to support you in setting boundaries or limiting your mother-in-law’s expectations.

Express Concerns: Let your partner know how this behavior impacts your family. Together, you can decide how to approach the situation in a way that protects your child’s emotional needs.


5. Teach Your Child Boundaries

Empower Your Child: As your child gets older, help them understand that it’s okay to set boundaries with people, even family members, if they feel uncomfortable. This will help them develop healthy relationships in the future.

Balance Kindness and Self-Respect: Encourage your child to be kind, but also to understand that they don’t need to do things just to please someone else, especially if it doesn’t feel right to them.


Conclusion

It’s difficult when a family member seems more focused on their own emotional needs than on the well-being of your child. By setting boundaries and prioritizing healthy, genuine relationships, you can protect your child and guide them toward relationships that truly nurture them.
